bāhyārthakṛta eva bhavatīti dṛḍhābhyāsavāsanāmahimnā prathamata eva prabhṛti sa ābhāsaḥ saṃvidi adhyavasāye ca nirbhāsamānaḥ samākṛṣṭa- bāhyatāka eva nirbhāsate mandamaterindrajālatimirādāviti prathamata eva prabhṛti bhrāntatvamuktam | (page 249) yastu timirādikāraṇatvamavaiti gacchan kakṣādyābhāsasya, sa bāhyatāṃ na adhyavasyati | tathāca nāvārūḍhaṃ paśya paśya taṭataravaḥ pratilomaṃ tūrṇaṃ tūrṇaṃ dhāvantīti savismayamācakṣāṇaṃ śiśukaṃ pratyāha naivaṃ vṛkṣā bhavanti, dṛśyate kevalamitthamiti | anena pratibhāsadharma eva ayamiti uktaṃ bhavati | evaṃ nirvikalpakena etat bādhiṣyamāṇabāhyatāsvīkārāt sahyamātmani bhrāntatvam, śuktirajatabhrame tu prathamanirvikalpakena rajata- svīkārābhāvāt na sahyamiti anyābhiprāyaḥ iti | tāvat iti | iha tāvadupayogi darśitam, anyattu darśayiṣyate | bhavatām iti svadarśane bhrāntitattvaṃ yat, tadiha na tāvat darśitamiti yāvat | yat nareśvaravivekaḥ pareṣāmapi keśādau bhrāntā saṃvidbahirmukhā | iti | evaṃ lokaprasiddhe bhramarūpe yastṛtīyo'dhyavasāyāṃśaḥ, tannidarśanena sarvatra adhyavasāye bhrāntirūpaṃ pradarśya bhrāntirūpeṇa adhyavasāyena vyavatiṣṭhāpayiṣitasya bāhyasya vyavasthā na ghaṭate tatra aṃśe tasya jaḍarūpatvāt | yatra aṃśe ca ajaḍatvamabāhye, tatra vyavasthāsaṃpādanānaut- sukyāditi darśayati smṛtijñānaṃ hi iti | hi iti yasmādevaṃbhūto'tra vibhāga itīti, tasmāt viṣayavyasthāpakatvamadhyavasāyasya na yujyate yathā prakṛtasya smṛtijñānasyeti | smṛtirupalakṣaṇamatra | etadeva ghaṭayati sa iti | yoṃ'śo na bhrānto nirvikalpakasvasaṃvedanalakṣaṇaḥ, sa na arthasya vyavasthāpakastena anyasyaiva svarūpasya svābhāsasya ca prakāśanāt | yataḥ soṃ'śaḥ pratibhāsamānaḥ svarūpasvābhāsasvabhāvaḥ, tasmāt smṛtijñānādabhinno na vyatiriktaḥ, na bāhyasvabhāvo (page 250) jñānādavyatiriktaṃ ca---------| iti nyāyāt | yastu vikalpanavyāpārātmā adhyavasāyaḥ, sa yadyapi svāṃśādavatīrṇa iva lakṣyate ityato'rthe vyavasthāpakatayā saṃbhāvayitumārabdhaḥ, tathāpi na nirvahati asya saṃbhāvanā | tadāha yāvatā iti pūrvapra
**The determination cannot reach outside** The Buddhist, having lost the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation, falls back on one last notion: the *determination* (adhyavasāya) — the act by which, he thinks, the cognition is taken to establish an external thing. Abhinavagupta now cuts this last thread. The determination, he shows, cannot establish anything outside. Consider how the "external" seems to appear. It is, Abhinavagupta says, only the strength of the firm practice-impression that makes the appearance seem drawn to an external object. From the very first, the appearance shining in the consciousness and in the determination is taken as external — but only for the slow-minded, in the illusion and the diseased-eye case. He who knows the cause of the appearance does not determine its externality at all. The child who cries in astonishment, "the trees on the far bank rush against the current!" is told: "it is not so — the trees do not rush; it is only seen so." The manifestation-dharma alone is this. The seeming outwardness is a manner of the seeing, not a thing established. And the determination itself, Abhinavagupta presses, is error-form. In every determination — even in the most ordinary case — there is this error-form, this drawing of the appearance outward. So the external, which the error-form determination was supposed to establish, has no standing in that very part: for the part is inert, and an inert thing cannot establish. And in the part that is not inert — the non-construction, the pure self-experience — there the establishment is not made either, for that part shines only its own form and its own self-appearance. So the determination's object-establishing power fails on both sides. The non-erroneous part, the self-experience, is un-divided from the memory-cognition — it is not a separate thing reaching out to an external — and so it is not external-natured. The Buddhist tries once more: "let the determination be both erroneous and establishing — what is the harm?" But this too fails, for the reason is the inertness: an inert thing cannot establish. And the last attempt — "as the fire burns the wood though inert, so the determination establishes the object; why this question of inert or conscious?" — is met: the establishing is in the self; the experience, with the manifestation at its head, is the establishing, and it is self-luminous, not a thing that reaches a thing. So the whole attempt to find a real external established by the determination collapses. The determination is only the manifestation-form in the self; the external is only drawn-to by the impression, never established; and the self-experience, un-divided from the memory-cognition, is the self-luminous awareness alone. The cognition never establishes a thing outside itself, because there is nothing outside the self-luminous awareness for it to reach. The self is one, self-luminous, and all — the memory, the determination, the experience — are its own shining. ---
